text: How does a steel box carry you up a hundred floors? Let's take an elevator apart.
This is a traction elevator. The car rides up and down the shaft, hung from steel hoist ropes.
Up top, the ropes wrap over a grooved wheel called the sheave. An electric motor turns it, and friction in the grooves does the lifting.
On the other end of the ropes hangs the counterweight. It weighs about as much as the car, plus forty percent of a full load.
So the motor never lifts the whole car. It only moves the difference.
Guide rails run the full height of the shaft, keeping the car and counterweight on track.
Codes require at least three hoist ropes, each built with a huge safety margin.
But what if the car starts falling? Up top, a governor watches the speed. Too fast, and it trips.
It grabs its own rope, which yanks the safety brakes. Steel wedges bite the guide rails and stop the car.
In eighteen fifty-four, in New York, Elisha Otis stood on a raised platform and had its rope cut. It dropped a few inches, then held.
